Chizu: A Minimal macOS Default Browser That Routes Links to Specific Profiles

04 Nov 2026, 06:37 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Editorial Desk · Source: github.com

Overview

Chizu is an open‑source utility for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 14 or later. It replaces the system’s default browser with a tiny app that does no rendering itself – it simply reads a set of rules from a JSONC configuration file and forwards each incoming URL to a browser of your choice, optionally selecting a named profile in Chrome, Dia or Firefox.

The project lives on GitHub (github.com/azu/chizu) under the MIT License and is distributed as a pre‑built ZIP that does not require Xcode, a signing certificate, or a notarisation step.

---

Installation

  1. Download the latest `chizu-macos-arm64.zip` from the GitHub releases page.
  2. Verify the SHA‑256 checksum provided alongside the ZIP.
  3. Run the bundled install script, which extracts the app to `~/Applications/Chizu.app` and clears the quarantine attribute with `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine`.
  4. The app is signed with a fixed self‑signed certificate; macOS will warn that it is not notarised – you must explicitly allow the app to run.

Note: If you already have a locally signed copy of Chizu, you may need to re‑grant Automation permission for Dia after the update.

Configuration

Create a starter file at `~/.config/chizu/config.jsonc`. A minimal example that falls back to Safari looks like this: ```jsonc { "version": "1.0", "default": { "browser": "com.apple.Safari" }, "rules": [] } ```

  • The file supports comments (`//` or `/* … */`) and trailing commas, thanks to the JSONC format.
  • Each rule consists of a name, a when object that defines matching conditions, and a destination that specifies the target browser bundle ID and, if applicable, a profile name.
  • Rules are evaluated top‑to‑bottom; the first matching rule wins.

You can edit the file with any editor and keep it under version control – the app rereads the file for every link, so no restart is needed.

---

How Routing Works

Source-listed details
ConditionExampleMeaning
`host``"example.com"`Exact host match
`pathPrefix``"/projects"`URL path must start with this string
`urlRegex``"(?i).*\\.pdf"`Case‑insensitive regex; matches URLs ending in `.pdf`
`sourceBundleID``"com.apple.mail"`Only apply when the sending app is Mail

A sample rule set might look like: ```jsonc { "rules": [ { "name": "Work Docs", "when": { "host": "docs.example.com" }, "destination": { "browser": "com.google.Chrome", "profile": "Work" } }, { "name": "Team Calendar", "when": { "host": "calendar.example.com", "sourceBundleID": "com.apple.mail" }, "destination": { "browser": "com.dia.Dia", "profile": "Team" } } ] } ``` If a rule references a Chrome or Firefox profile that does not exist, Chizu reports an error instead of silently falling back to another profile.

---

Limitations & Security Considerations

  • No UI – there is no preferences window or browser picker; all behaviour is driven by the JSONC file.
  • Automation permissions – the first time a rule tries to control Dia, macOS will ask for Automation access. Denying it results in an error message.
  • File‑system access – reading Chrome’s *Local State* or Firefox’s *profiles.ini* requires the user to grant “Files and Folders” access in System Settings → Privacy & Security.
  • Self‑signed certificate – because the app is not notarised, macOS treats it as an unsigned developer app. Users must manually allow it, and future macOS updates could tighten this requirement.
  • No fallback – if a rule’s destination browser is missing, Chizu aborts with an error; it never falls back to the default destination.

---

Practical Tips for Users

  • Test a rule without changing the system default: `~/Applications/Chizu.app/Contents/MacOS/chizu check https://example.com --source com.apple.mail` prints the matched rule, browser and profile.
  • Preview the routing before committing a large rule set: the `check` command validates JSON syntax and reports missing profiles.
  • Keep the config in your dotfiles: because the file is read on every link, you can version‑control it and tweak it on the fly.
  • Hand‑off from browsers: a userscript can replace `http:` with `chizu-http:`; Chizu strips the prefix and routes the link according to the same rules.
  • Reset permissions if a browser suddenly loses access: `tccutil reset SystemPolicyAppDataDetailed dev.azu.chizu` clears the stored consent.

---

How to Verify the Original Announcement

  1. Visit the official GitHub repository at github.com/azu/chizu.
  2. Check the Releases tab for the latest version tag and accompanying `SHA‑256` checksum file.
  3. Compare the checksum of the downloaded ZIP with the published value using `shasum -a 256`.
  4. Review the `README.md` and `docs/` folder for the authoritative description of features and installation steps.
  5. For security‑related concerns, inspect the `release-signing.json` and the fixed self‑signed certificate included in the repo.
